title: World Politics: Contemporary Centres of Power

topics.title: New centres of power and the roots of European unity

learn.hook: After 1991 one superpower stood tall. Yet regional groupings and fast-growing economies began building their own power, and Europe led the way.
points: After the Cold War, regional organisations (such as the EU and ASEAN) and rising states (such as China) emerged as alternative centres of political and economic power, limiting US dominance.
These centres draw their influence mainly from economic strength and from regional cooperation that turns neighbours from rivals into partners.

After the Second World War, Europe's economies were ruined. Under the Marshall Plan, the USA gave massive financial help, and the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC) was set up in 1948 to channel this aid.
The Council of Europe was set up in 1949, another step in political cooperation among European states.
Cooperation began with economics: the European Coal and Steel Community (1951) linked six western European countries.

example.q: Why did the OEEC matter for European integration?
steps: It was created in 1948 to distribute Marshall Plan aid.
To get aid, western European states had to sit together and coordinate trade and economic issues.
This habit of working together laid the base for later bodies like the EEC.
example.answer: It made western European states cooperate on economic matters, paving the way for integration

learn.reallife: India's own push for regional groupings, from SAARC to BIMSTEC, comes from the same idea: economic cooperation can build political trust among neighbours.

Answer: 1949

steps: Fact: after the Cold War, the EU, ASEAN and China emerged as alternative centres of power.

Answer: The European Union
quiz.mistake: Picks bodies that had ended or were weak

quiz.explain: Their power rests largely on economic integration and cooperation.
steps: Fact: new centres of power draw influence mainly from economic strength.
Regional cooperation turns neighbours from rivals into partners.
So economic strength and regional cooperation, not nuclear weapons alone.
Answer: Economic strength and regional cooperation
quiz.mistake: Thinks power comes only from military might

quiz.explain: Six countries formed it: France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

Answer: 6

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

quiz.explain: Both true; combined economic weight is what lets them act as counterweights.
steps: A: true — regional groups can limit a single superpower's dominance.
R: true — they pool members' economic strength.
R explains A: pooled strength is what makes them a counterweight.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link pooled strength with influence

teach.nudge: Good. But how did Europe begin its unity after the war? Think of US aid.

topics.title: From the EEC to the European Union

learn.hook: A German student can study in Spain, pay in euros and travel to France without showing a passport. That everyday freedom grew out of decades of treaties.
points: The Treaty of Rome (1957) set up the European Economic Community (EEC). Over time it deepened economic and political cooperation.
The European Union (EU) was established by the Maastricht Treaty, signed in 1992. It moved from an economic union towards a political one.
The EU set up a single market, a common foreign and security policy, cooperation on justice and home affairs, and a single currency.
The euro was introduced in 2002 as notes and coins in twelve member states, and is used by many EU members.
Like a state, the EU has its own flag, anthem, founding date and currency. Its flag is a circle of twelve gold stars on a blue background, standing for unity and harmony among the peoples of Europe.

example.q: Order these milestones: euro notes and coins introduced; Treaty of Rome sets up the EEC; Maastricht Treaty creates the EU.
steps: Treaty of Rome: 1957.
Maastricht Treaty: 1992.
Euro notes and coins: 2002.

learn.reallife: Indian tourists and students in Europe often need just one Schengen visa and one currency to cross many borders, a direct result of EU integration.

topics.title: The EU as a power and its limits

learn.hook: The EU can block a merger between two American tech giants, yet its members still argue over whether to send soldiers abroad. That is power with limits.
points: Economic power: the EU is one of the largest economies in the world, and its currency, the euro, can rival the US dollar. Its share of world trade is very large.

Political and diplomatic power: France, an EU member, is a permanent member of the UN Security Council, and several EU members serve as non-permanent members. The EU influences the US and others on trade and climate.
Military power: the combined armed forces of EU members are among the largest in the world, and France is a nuclear power. The EU is also strong in space and communication technology.
Limits: members keep their own foreign and defence policies and often disagree. There is Euroscepticism, as some people resist giving more power to the EU.
In 2016 the UK voted in a referendum to leave the EU, and it formally left in 2020 (Brexit).

example.q: Classify each as economic, political or military power of the EU: euro rivals the dollar; France has a UNSC permanent seat; France is a nuclear power.
steps: Euro rivalling the dollar: economic.
UNSC permanent seat: political/diplomatic.
Nuclear weapons: military.

learn.reallife: When the EU negotiates a trade deal with India, it bargains as one bloc of many economies. That is why the India-EU free trade talks are so closely watched in Indian markets.

learn.hook: In 1967 five nervous neighbours in Southeast Asia signed a short declaration in Bangkok. Decades later their group is among the most important regional bodies in Asia.
points: ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) was set up in 1967 by Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand, by signing the Bangkok Declaration. Others such as Brunei, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and Cambodia joined later.
Its aims: speed up economic growth, social progress and cultural development, and promote regional peace and stability based on the rule of law and the UN Charter.
The 'ASEAN Way' is a style of working that is informal, non-confrontational and cooperative, and that respects national sovereignty.
In 2003 ASEAN agreed to set up an ASEAN Community with three pillars: the ASEAN Security Community, the ASEAN Economic Community and the ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community.
The ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF), set up in 1994, carries out coordination on security and foreign policy.

example.q: Name the three pillars of the ASEAN Community agreed in 2003.
steps: Pillar 1: Security Community (peace, settling disputes without armed conflict).
Pillar 2: Economic Community (common market and production base).
Pillar 3: Socio-Cultural Community.

learn.reallife: Indian leaders attend ASEAN summits regularly, and Indian classical arts and Ramayana traditions are celebrated across Thailand, Indonesia and Cambodia, linking cultures as well as trade.

topics.title: ASEAN's economy and India's Look East policy

learn.hook: Many cars, phones and garments you buy carry parts made across Southeast Asia. ASEAN's economic engine is humming right in India's neighbourhood.
points: ASEAN is one of the fastest-growing regions in the world. Its economic community aims at a common market and production base and aids social and economic development.
The ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA) and the ASEAN Investment Area aim to lower trade barriers and attract investment.
ASEAN Vision 2020 set out an outward-looking role for ASEAN in the international community, building on its policy of encouraging negotiation over conflict.

In the early 1990s (usually dated to 1991, under the P.V. Narasimha Rao government) India adopted a Look East policy to strengthen ties with Southeast Asia, signed free trade agreements with Singapore and Thailand, and later an ASEAN-India free trade agreement. Since 2014 this has been carried forward as the Act East policy.
ASEAN's economic and strategic importance makes it an attractive partner for China, Japan, the USA and India.

example.q: Why did India turn its foreign policy towards ASEAN in the 1990s?
steps: After 1991 India opened its economy and sought new trade partners.
ASEAN was a fast-growing economic region next door.
Closer ties could bring trade, investment and strategic balance.
example.answer: To gain from ASEAN's fast-growing economy through trade, investment and strategic ties (Look East policy)

learn.reallife: India's North-Eastern states, such as Manipur and Mizoram, are seen as India's gateway to Southeast Asia, which is why road and port projects towards Myanmar matter under the Act East policy.

quiz.mistake: Confuses the start of Look East with Act East

quiz.q: With which ASEAN countries did India sign bilateral free trade agreements?
quiz.explain: These two were India's early FTA partners in ASEAN.
steps: Fact: India signed free trade agreements with Singapore and Thailand.
Japan, Korea, Nepal, Bhutan, China and Mongolia are not ASEAN members.
So Singapore and Thailand.
Answer: Singapore and Thailand
quiz.mistake: Names countries outside ASEAN

quiz.q: Which statement about ASEAN's economy is correct?
options: It has a single currency like the euro
Its members have no trade with each other
It is one of the fastest-growing regions in the world
It is smaller than any single Indian state
quiz.explain: ASEAN's rapid growth makes it an attractive partner.
steps: Fact: ASEAN is one of the fastest-growing regions in the world.
It has no single currency like the euro, and members do trade with each other.
So it is one of the fastest-growing regions.
Answer: It is one of the fastest-growing regions in the world
quiz.mistake: Assumes ASEAN copies the EU in every way

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Many big powers seek closer ties with ASEAN. Reason (R): ASEAN is economically dynamic and strategically placed.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; its economic and strategic importance attracts outside powers.
steps: A: true — China, Japan, the USA and India seek ties with ASEAN.
R: true — ASEAN is economically dynamic and strategically placed.
R explains A: that importance is why big powers court it.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Misses the reason outside powers court ASEAN

quiz.q: Case: An Indian company sets up a factory in Thailand to sell across Southeast Asia with lower tariffs. Which ASEAN arrangement helps it most?
quiz.explain: AFTA lowers tariffs among members, helping firms sell across the region.
steps: The firm wants to sell across Southeast Asia with lower tariffs.
AFTA aims to lower trade barriers among members; the ARF is about security.
So the ASEAN Free Trade Area helps it most.
Answer: The ASEAN Free Trade Area
quiz.mistake: Picks the security forum instead of the trade area

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does India care so much about ASEAN? It's not even in South Asia!'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! ASEAN is a fast-growing economy with free trade, so India's Look East and Act East policies built strong ties!
teach.nudge: Good. What is the name of India's policy towards ASEAN?

revise.summary: ASEAN is one of the fastest-growing regions, with AFTA and an Investment Area to cut barriers and Vision 2020 for an outward role. India's Look East policy (1991), carried forward as Act East (2014), built trade ties including FTAs with Singapore and Thailand.
focus: ASEAN's economic arrangements
India's Look East and Act East policies
Why big powers court ASEAN
remember: AFTA = ASEAN Free Trade Area
Look East from 1991; Act East since 2014
Early FTAs with Singapore and Thailand
traps: Don't confuse the start of Look East (1991) with Act East (2014).
ASEAN has no single currency like the euro.

learn.hook: In 1978 China was poorer than India on many measures. A generation later it was the world's factory. The turnaround began with one leader's decision to open the door.
points: After the communist revolution of 1949 under Mao Zedong, China followed the Soviet model: state-owned heavy industries were built using capital from agriculture, and China cut off links with the capitalist world.

This model gave limited growth: industrial production did not grow fast enough, agricultural output was too low to support industry, and foreign trade was minimal. In 1973 Zhou Enlai proposed four modernisations: agriculture, industry, science and technology, and the military.
In 1978 Deng Xiaoping announced the 'open door' policy, aiming to generate higher productivity by inviting foreign capital and technology.
China did not use shock therapy; it opened up step by step. Agriculture was privatised in 1982 and industry in 1998.
Special Economic Zones (SEZs) were set up where foreign investors could set up businesses, and trade barriers were eased there first.

example.q: Compare: How did China's reform path differ from Russia's shock therapy?
steps: Russia: sudden, all-at-once switch to capitalism in the 1990s.
China: gradual opening from 1978 — agriculture privatised in 1982, industry in 1998, SEZs first.
China kept its political system while changing the economy step by step.
example.answer: China reformed gradually and in stages, while Russia used sudden shock therapy

learn.reallife: India copied the SEZ idea in its own SEZ Act of 2005, and export hubs in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu show the same logic of special zones for investors.

items.text: China's 'open door' policy was announced by ___ in 1978.
Agriculture in China was privatised in ___.
Industry in China was privatised in ___.
Foreign investors could set up firms in Special Economic ___.

quiz.q: Who announced China's 'open door' policy in 1978?
quiz.explain: Deng launched market reforms and opened China to foreign capital.
steps: Asked: who announced the open door policy in 1978.
Fact: Deng Xiaoping announced it to invite foreign capital and technology.
Mao led the earlier socialist phase, so he does not fit.
Answer: Deng Xiaoping
quiz.mistake: Credits Mao, who led the earlier socialist phase

quiz.q: After 1949, China's economy was modelled on:
quiz.explain: China built state-owned heavy industry like the USSR.
steps: Fact: after the 1949 revolution under Mao, China followed the Soviet model.
It built state-owned heavy industries and cut links with the capitalist world.
So the Soviet model.
Answer: The Soviet model
quiz.mistake: Assumes China was always market-oriented

quiz.q: Agriculture in China was privatised in:
quiz.explain: Farming was privatised in 1982, before industry.
steps: China opened up step by step after 1978.
Fact: agriculture was privatised in 1982, industry in 1998.
Answer: 1982
quiz.mistake: Confuses the open door year with farm privatisation

quiz.q: Which did China privatise in 1998?
quiz.explain: Industry followed agriculture, in 1998.
steps: Order of privatisation: agriculture first (1982), then industry.
Fact: industry was privatised in 1998.
So industry.
Answer: Industry
quiz.mistake: Swaps the order of privatisation

quiz.q: Who proposed the 'four modernisations' in 1973?
quiz.explain: Zhou Enlai proposed modernising agriculture, industry, science and technology, and the military.
steps: Fact: in 1973 Zhou Enlai proposed the four modernisations.
Deng came later with the open door policy (1978).
So Zhou Enlai.
Answer: Zhou Enlai
quiz.mistake: Credits Deng with every reform idea

quiz.q: Which of these was one of the four modernisations?
quiz.explain: The four were agriculture, industry, science and technology, and the military.
steps: The four modernisations: agriculture, industry, science and technology, military.
Religion, tourism and monarchy are not on the list.
So science and technology.
Answer: Science and technology
quiz.mistake: Picks an item outside the list

quiz.q: Assertion (A): China did not follow shock therapy. Reason (R): It opened its economy step by step, starting with agriculture and Special Economic Zones.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the gradual, staged approach is the opposite of shock therapy.
steps: A: true — China did not use shock therapy.
R: true — it opened step by step: agriculture 1982, SEZs, industry 1998.
R explains A: gradual opening is the opposite of shock therapy.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks China and Russia reformed the same way

quiz.q: Assertion (A): China's early Soviet-style model produced very fast growth in agriculture. Reason (R): Under this model, China had cut its links with the capitalist world.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: agricultural output stayed low. R is true.
steps: A: false — under the early model agricultural output was too low.
R: true — China had cut links with the capitalist world.
So A is false, but R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true
quiz.mistake: Overrates the results of the early model

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How did China change from a closed economy to a giant one? What were the steps?'
teach.praise: Wow! Soviet model after 1949, Deng's open door in 1978, then privatising farms in 1982 and industry in 1998, with SEZs. Step by step!
teach.nudge: Nice. Who opened the door in 1978? And did China change suddenly or gradually?

revise.summary: After 1949 China followed the Soviet model with limited growth. Zhou Enlai proposed four modernisations (1973) and Deng Xiaoping's open door policy (1978) opened China step by step: agriculture privatised 1982, industry 1998, with SEZs.
focus: China's early Soviet-style model and its limits
Open door policy and gradual reforms
How China differed from shock therapy
remember: Deng Xiaoping: open door, 1978
Agriculture privatised 1982; industry 1998
Four modernisations: agriculture, industry, science and technology, military
traps: Mao did not launch the open door policy.
China did not use shock therapy; it reformed gradually.
Don't swap the order of farm (1982) and industry (1998) privatisation.

topics.title: China as a global economic power: gains and problems

learn.hook: From toys to solar panels to smartphones, 'Made in China' is everywhere. But growth at that speed came with a bill.
points: China joined the World Trade Organisation in 2001, further opening its economy to the world. Foreign trade and investment grew rapidly.
China became a huge economy and a major destination for foreign direct investment, with large foreign exchange reserves.
Problems: not everyone benefited. There was unemployment, environmental degradation, corruption and rising inequality between rural and urban areas and between coastal and inland regions.

China's economic weight increased its regional and global influence. It built economic ties with its neighbours, including ASEAN states, Japan and South Korea, and its trade with the USA and India grew.

example.q: Sort into gains and problems of China's reforms: foreign investment; inequality between coast and inland; WTO entry; environmental damage.
steps: Gains: foreign investment, WTO entry (integration into world trade).
Problems: regional inequality, environmental damage.
example.answer: Gains: investment, WTO entry; Problems: inequality, pollution

learn.reallife: Indian cities like Delhi face air-quality crises too; China's experience shows how fast industrial growth can come at a heavy environmental cost if not managed.

games.title: True or false?
items: This deepened its integration with the world economy.
All Chinese regions benefited equally from reforms.
Coastal and urban areas gained more than inland and rural areas.
Environmental damage was a cost of China's growth.
China's growth reduced its influence in Asia.
Its economic weight increased its regional influence.

quiz.q: China became a member of the World Trade Organisation in:
quiz.explain: China's WTO entry came in 2001.
steps: Asked: when China joined the WTO.
Fact: China joined in 2001, opening its economy further.
1995 is when the WTO itself began, a tempting wrong choice.
Answer: 2001
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the WTO's founding year (1995)

quiz.q: Which of these is a problem that came with China's economic reforms?
options: Rising inequality between coastal and inland regions
quiz.explain: Benefits were uneven, and inequality grew.
steps: Fact: problems of reform included unemployment, pollution, corruption and rising inequality.
Foreign investment and exports actually grew.
So rising inequality between coastal and inland regions.
Answer: Rising inequality between coastal and inland regions
quiz.mistake: Assumes rapid growth benefits everyone equally

quiz.q: Which region of China gained more from reforms?
quiz.explain: Coastal areas with SEZs and ports drew most investment.
steps: Fact: inequality grew between coastal and inland regions.
Coastal areas with SEZs and ports drew most investment.
So coastal areas gained more.
Answer: Coastal areas
quiz.mistake: Ignores regional inequality

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a problem of China's growth?
quiz.explain: China actually became a major destination for foreign investment.
steps: Listed problems: unemployment, environmental degradation, corruption, inequality.
China became a major destination for foreign investment.
So a shortage of foreign investment is NOT a problem.
Answer: A shortage of foreign investment
quiz.mistake: Picks something China had in abundance

quiz.q: How did China's economic growth affect its position in Asia?
options: It isolated China from its neighbours
It made China join the EU
It ended China's trade with India
quiz.explain: Economic power brought greater regional and global influence.
steps: Fact: China's economic weight increased its regional and global influence.
It built economic ties with ASEAN, Japan, South Korea and others.
So it increased China's regional influence.
Answer: It increased China's regional influence
quiz.mistake: Thinks growth reduced influence

quiz.q: Joining the WTO meant that China:
options: Opened its economy further to world trade
Ended state control of the military
quiz.explain: WTO membership required further opening of trade.
steps: The WTO is about world trade.
Fact: joining in 2001 further opened China's economy.
So China opened its economy further to world trade.
Answer: Opened its economy further to world trade
quiz.mistake: Misreads the purpose of the WTO

quiz.q: Assertion (A): China's economic rise has made it an important centre of power. Reason (R): China has become a major destination for foreign investment and trade.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; its economic weight explains its new status.
steps: A: true — China's rise made it a centre of power.
R: true — it became a major destination for foreign investment and trade.
R explains A: its economic weight gives it power.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link economic growth to political influence

quiz.q: Assertion (A): China's reforms reduced all forms of inequality. Reason (R): Coastal regions and cities gained more from the reforms than rural and inland areas.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false; R is true and shows inequality grew.
steps: A: false — inequality rose, it did not fall.
R: true — coastal and urban areas gained more than rural and inland areas.
So A is false, but R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true
quiz.mistake: Ignores uneven distribution of benefits

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'China got rich, so everyone there must be happy, right?'
teach.praise: Hmm! China joined the WTO in 2001 and became a giant, but faced inequality, pollution and corruption. Growth isn't the whole story!
teach.nudge: Okay, but what were the problems that came along with all that growth?

revise.summary: China joined the WTO in 2001 and became a huge economy and investment destination, raising its regional and global influence, but reforms brought unemployment, pollution, corruption and inequality between coast and inland.
focus: Gains of China's reforms
Problems of China's growth
Effect on China's influence
remember: China joined the WTO in 2001
Coastal areas gained more than inland and rural areas
China is a major destination for foreign investment
traps: Reforms did not reduce inequality; they widened it.
China did not suffer a shortage of foreign investment.

topics.title: India and China: rivalry and cooperation

learn.hook: Buddhist monks carried ideas across the Himalayas two thousand years ago. In 1962 soldiers fought on those same mountains. India-China ties have swung between both extremes.
points: India and China had old cultural and economic links, such as the spread of Buddhism and trade along routes across Asia. After independence, relations began warmly with the slogan 'Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai'.
The military conflict of 1962 over a border dispute damaged relations badly. Full diplomatic relations were restored only in 1976.
Rajiv Gandhi's visit to China in December 1988 began a process of normalisation. Both sides agreed to work on the border issue through talks and to expand other ties.
Trade between India and China has grown very fast, and they cooperate in many multilateral forums, such as on trade talks and climate change.
Differences remain over the border, China's close ties with Pakistan, and competition for influence in the region.

example.q: Put these in order: Rajiv Gandhi visits China; India-China war; full diplomatic relations restored.
steps: 1962: India-China war.
1976: full diplomatic relations restored.
1988: Rajiv Gandhi's visit.

learn.reallife: Many electronics parts used by Indian startups and phone makers are imported from China, while India pushes 'Make in India' to reduce this dependence. Cooperation and rivalry run side by side.

quiz.q: The military conflict between India and China took place in:
quiz.explain: The border war was fought in 1962.
steps: Asked: the year of the India–China war.
Fact: the border conflict was fought in 1962.
1965 and 1971 were India–Pakistan wars.
Answer: 1962
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the India-Pakistan wars

quiz.q: Whose visit to China in 1988 began normalisation of India-China relations?
quiz.explain: Rajiv Gandhi visited in December 1988.
steps: Fact: Rajiv Gandhi's visit to China in December 1988 began normalisation.
Nehru led India in 1962; the visit came much later.
So Rajiv Gandhi.
Answer: Rajiv Gandhi
quiz.mistake: Picks a different Prime Minister

quiz.q: After the 1962 conflict, full diplomatic relations between India and China were restored in:
quiz.explain: Ambassador-level relations were restored in 1976; Rajiv Gandhi's visit came in 1988.
steps: After the 1962 war relations were badly damaged.
Fact: full diplomatic relations were restored only in 1976.
1988 is Rajiv Gandhi's visit, a tempting wrong choice.
Answer: 1976
quiz.mistake: Confuses restoration of relations with the 1988 visit

quiz.q: Which of these is a continuing source of friction between India and China?
quiz.explain: The unresolved border remains a major issue.
steps: Fact: differences remain over the border, China's ties with Pakistan and regional competition.
Buddhism links them; they share no currency and are not ASEAN members.
So the border dispute.
Answer: The border dispute
quiz.mistake: Picks a non-issue

quiz.q: Which statement best describes India-China relations today?
options: A mix of competition and cooperation
quiz.explain: They trade heavily and cooperate in forums, yet compete and dispute the border.
steps: They trade heavily and cooperate in forums on trade and climate.
They also dispute the border and compete for influence.
So a mix of competition and cooperation.
Answer: A mix of competition and cooperation
quiz.mistake: Sees only one side of the relationship

quiz.q: The slogan of warm India-China ties in the 1950s was:
quiz.explain: This slogan captured early friendship.
steps: Fact: early warm ties were summed up as 'Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai'.
The other slogans are from Indian domestic politics or later policy.
So Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai.
Answer: Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai
quiz.mistake: Picks a slogan from Indian domestic politics

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Trade between India and China has grown fast since the 1990s. Reason (R): India and China fought a border war in 1962.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both statements are true, but the 1962 war does not explain the growth of trade.
steps: A: true — India–China trade has grown very fast.
R: true — they fought a border war in 1962.
But R does not explain A: the 1962 war is not why trade grew.
Answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Treats two unrelated true facts as cause and effect

quiz.q: Assertion (A): India and China cooperate in multilateral forums. Reason (R): India and China have resolved all their border disputes.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: the border question remains unresolved.
steps: A: true — they cooperate in multilateral forums.
R: false — the border dispute is still unresolved.
So A is true, but R is false.
Answer: A is true, but R is false
quiz.mistake: Assumes cooperation means all disputes are settled

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Are India and China friends or rivals? I'm confused!'
teach.praise: Got it! Old links, a 1962 war, normalising from Rajiv Gandhi's 1988 visit, booming trade, but the border dispute remains. Both friends and rivals!
teach.nudge: You said they fought. What changed after 1988, and what still divides them?

revise.summary: India and China had old links and warm 1950s ties ('Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai'), damaged by the 1962 war. Relations were restored in 1976, normalisation began with Rajiv Gandhi's 1988 visit, and today they mix fast-growing trade and cooperation with border disputes and rivalry.
focus: Order of key events in India–China relations
Areas of cooperation and of friction
remember: 1962 war; 1976 full relations restored; 1988 Rajiv Gandhi visit
Friction: border, China–Pakistan ties, regional rivalry
Cooperation: trade and multilateral forums
traps: Don't confuse 1976 (relations restored) with 1988 (Rajiv Gandhi's visit).
Cooperation does not mean the border dispute is settled.

topics.title: Japan and South Korea as emerging powers

learn.hook: Your family car might be a Suzuki or Hyundai, your TV a Sony or Samsung. Two East Asian nations built global brands from post-war ruins.
points: Japan has few natural resources and imports most raw materials, yet it became a leading economic and technological power, with brands like Sony, Panasonic, Canon, Toyota, Honda and Suzuki. It is a member of the G-7 (formerly G-8).

Japan is the only country to have suffered nuclear bombing (Hiroshima and Nagasaki, 1945). Article 9 of its Constitution renounces war as a sovereign right, so its military role is limited. Japan is one of the largest contributors to the UN budget.

South Korea grew rapidly from the 1960s to the 1980s. This rise is called the 'Miracle on the Han River'. Factors included land reform, rural development, investment in human resources and rapid industrialisation.
South Korea joined the OECD in 1996 and is a member of the G-20. Its global brands include Samsung, LG and Hyundai.
Comparing centres of power: the EU and ASEAN are regional groups that pool members' strength, while China, Japan and South Korea are individual states that rose through economic growth.

example.q: Board-style: Give two reasons why Japan is considered an important centre of power.
steps: Economic and technological strength with global brands, despite few natural resources.
Major contributor to the UN budget and member of the G-7.
(Its military role is limited by Article 9.)
example.answer: Strong technology-based economy; major UN funder and G-7 member

learn.reallife: Japan has funded the Delhi Metro and the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail project, while Korean firms like Hyundai and Samsung run big factories in Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh.

games.title: Match the fact
pairs: South Korea joins the club of rich economies

quiz.q: Which article of Japan's Constitution renounces war as a sovereign right?
quiz.explain: Article 9 limits Japan's military role.
steps: Fact: Article 9 of Japan's Constitution renounces war as a sovereign right.
Articles 51 and 370 are linked to other texts, not Japan.
So Article 9.
Answer: Article 9
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with Indian constitutional articles

quiz.q: Japan is the only country to have suffered:
quiz.explain: Hiroshima and Nagasaki were bombed in 1945.
steps: Fact: Japan is the only country to have suffered nuclear bombing.
Hiroshima and Nagasaki were bombed in 1945.
So destruction by nuclear bombs.
Answer: Destruction by nuclear bombs
quiz.mistake: Confuses Japan with Korea or Germany

quiz.q: The term 'Miracle on the Han River' refers to:
quiz.explain: It describes South Korea's fast industrial rise.
steps: Fact: South Korea's rapid growth from the 1960s to 1980s is called the 'Miracle on the Han River'.
It is not about Japan or China.
So South Korea's rapid economic growth.
Answer: South Korea's rapid economic growth
quiz.mistake: Links it to Japan

quiz.q: South Korea became a member of the OECD in:
quiz.explain: It joined the OECD in 1996.
steps: Fact: South Korea joined the OECD in 1996.
1991 is the year both Koreas joined the UN, a tempting wrong choice.
Answer: 1996
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the year both Koreas joined the UN (1991)

quiz.q: Which is true of Japan's natural resources?
options: It has few natural resources and imports most raw materials
It is the world's largest oil exporter
It has the largest coal reserves in Asia
It needs no imports at all
quiz.explain: Japan's power rests on technology and industry, not natural resources.
steps: Fact: Japan has few natural resources and imports most raw materials.
Its power rests on technology and industry.
So it has few natural resources and imports most raw materials.
Answer: It has few natural resources and imports most raw materials
quiz.mistake: Assumes economic power needs natural resources

quiz.q: Which factor helped South Korea's rapid development?
options: Land reform and investment in human resources
quiz.explain: Land reform, rural development, human resources and industrialisation fuelled growth.
steps: Fact: South Korea's growth came from land reform, rural development, human resources and industrialisation.
Isolation or rejecting industry would slow growth.
So land reform and investment in human resources.
Answer: Land reform and investment in human resources
quiz.mistake: Picks factors that would slow growth

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Japan's military role is limited. Reason (R): Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution renounces war as a sovereign right.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; Article 9 explains the limited military role.
steps: A: true — Japan's military role is limited.
R: true — Article 9 renounces war as a sovereign right.
R explains A: the constitution limits its military role.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the constitutional clause with military limits

quiz.q: Case: A class compares the EU with Japan as 'centres of power'. Which difference is correct?
options: The EU is a regional union of states; Japan is a single state
The EU has one army and Japan has none
quiz.explain: The EU pools many states' strength, whereas Japan is one country that rose through its economy.
steps: The EU is a regional group that pools the strength of many states.
Japan is one country that rose through economic growth.
So the EU is a regional union of states; Japan is a single state.
Answer: The EU is a regional union of states; Japan is a single state
quiz.mistake: Treats a country and a regional union as the same kind of actor

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Japan and South Korea are small. How can they be centres of power?'
teach.praise: Yay! Japan and South Korea built mighty economies and technology. Japan's military is limited by Article 9, and Korea had its Han River miracle!
teach.nudge: Good. What limits Japan's military? And what is South Korea's growth story called?

revise.summary: Japan, with few natural resources, became a leading technological economy and big UN funder, with a military limited by Article 9. South Korea's rapid rise, the 'Miracle on the Han River', came from land reform, human resources and industrialisation; it joined the OECD in 1996.
focus: Why Japan is a centre of power
Causes of South Korea's growth
How states differ from regional unions as centres of power
remember: Article 9 renounces war as a sovereign right
Japan: only country to suffer nuclear bombing (1945)
South Korea joined the OECD in 1996
traps: The 'Miracle on the Han River' is South Korea, not Japan.
Economic power does not need natural resources.
Japan is a single state, the EU a regional union.
